exam.title: Session 7 — Python Practice
exam.description: 40-question source-scoped practice for File Handling, OS Module & File System Operations.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `open() & Modes` according to the taught session?

options.text: `open(path, mode)` opens a file; default mode is read (`r`) if omitted.
`file.close()` closes a file object and releases resources; `f.closed` reports whether it is closed.
`read()` reads file content; `read(n)` can read only a limited number of characters.
A `with` statement automatically handles closing the file and reduces resource-leak risk.

explanation.ar: `open(path, mode)` opens a file; default mode is read (`r`) if omitted.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to open a file in a chosen mode?

options.text: file.close()
open("file.txt", "r")
file.read() / file.read(n)
with open(...) as file:

explanation.ar: `open("file.txt", "r")` is the course-aligned choice for this task: open a file in a chosen mode.

questions.question: What is the default mode if `open()` is called without an explicit mode?

options.text: w
a
r
x

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `open() & Modes` behavior: `open(path, mode)` opens a file; default mode is read (`r`) if omitted.

questions.question: A learner uses write mode when they only intend to read an existing file. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `file.close()` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `open() & Modes` has no rules.
Convert the task to `read()` without changing the logic.
Choose read mode (`r`) for reading rather than a destructive write mode.

explanation.ar: Choose read mode (`r`) for reading rather than a destructive write mode.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `close()` according to the taught session?

options.text: `file.close()` closes a file object and releases resources; `f.closed` reports whether it is closed.
`read()` reads file content; `read(n)` can read only a limited number of characters.
A `with` statement automatically handles closing the file and reduces resource-leak risk.
`w` truncates existing content before writing; `a` appends at the end without removing existing content.

explanation.ar: `file.close()` closes a file object and releases resources; `f.closed` reports whether it is closed.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to close a high-level file object?

options.text: file.read() / file.read(n)
file.close()
with open(...) as file:
"w" vs "a"

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. `file.close()` is the course-aligned choice for this task: close a high-level file object.

questions.question: After calling `f.close()`, what should `f.closed` report?

options.text: False
True
The filename

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `close()` behavior: `file.close()` closes a file object and releases resources; `f.closed` reports whether it is closed.

questions.question: A learner uses `os.close(file_object)` on a file object created with `open()`. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `file.read() / file.read(n)` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `close()` has no rules.
Convert the task to `with Statement` without changing the logic.
Use `file.close()` for a normal file object; `os.close()` expects a low-level integer descriptor.

explanation.ar: Use `file.close()` for a normal file object; `os.close()` expects a low-level integer descriptor.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `read()` according to the taught session?

options.text: `read()` reads file content; `read(n)` can read only a limited number of characters.
A `with` statement automatically handles closing the file and reduces resource-leak risk.
`w` truncates existing content before writing; `a` appends at the end without removing existing content.
The current working directory is where relative file operations are resolved; `os.getcwd()` reads it and `os.chdir()` changes it.

explanation.ar: `read()` reads file content; `read(n)` can read only a limited number of characters.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to read all or a limited part of a file?

options.text: with open(...) as file:
file.read() / file.read(n)
"w" vs "a"
os.getcwd() / os.chdir(path)

explanation.ar: `file.read() / file.read(n)` is the course-aligned choice for this task: read all or a limited part of a file.

questions.question: What does `file.read(10)` request?

options.text: 10 lines necessarily
A 10-byte file creation
The first/next 10 characters from the current position
10 directory names

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. The trace follows the taught `read()` behavior: `read()` reads file content; `read(n)` can read only a limited number of characters.

questions.question: A learner loads an entire huge file when only a small preview is needed. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `with open(...) as file:` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `read()` has no rules.
Convert the task to `Write vs Append` without changing the logic.
Use a limited read or line-by-line iteration when appropriate.

explanation.ar: Use a limited read or line-by-line iteration when appropriate.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `with Statement` according to the taught session?

options.text: A `with` statement automatically handles closing the file and reduces resource-leak risk.
`w` truncates existing content before writing; `a` appends at the end without removing existing content.
The current working directory is where relative file operations are resolved; `os.getcwd()` reads it and `os.chdir()` changes it.
`os.mkdir()` creates one directory; `os.makedirs()` can create missing intermediate directories recursively.

explanation.ar: A `with` statement automatically handles closing the file and reduces resource-leak risk.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to open a file with automatic cleanup?

options.text: "w" vs "a"
with open(...) as file:
os.getcwd() / os.chdir(path)
os.mkdir() / os.makedirs()

explanation.ar: `with open(...) as file:` is the course-aligned choice for this task: open a file with automatic cleanup.

questions.question: What happens to the file after leaving a correctly used `with open(...)` block?

options.text: It remains permanently open
It is automatically deleted
It is automatically closed.
It becomes a directory

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `with Statement` behavior: A `with` statement automatically handles closing the file and reduces resource-leak risk.

questions.question: A learner copies the source typo `withopen` as if it were valid Python syntax. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `"w" vs "a"` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `with Statement` has no rules.
Convert the task to `CWD` without changing the logic.
Use the valid syntax `with open(...) as file:`; the slide spacing is a presentation typo.

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. Use the valid syntax `with open(...) as file:`; the slide spacing is a presentation typo.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `Write vs Append` according to the taught session?

options.text: `w` truncates existing content before writing; `a` appends at the end without removing existing content.
The current working directory is where relative file operations are resolved; `os.getcwd()` reads it and `os.chdir()` changes it.
`os.mkdir()` creates one directory; `os.makedirs()` can create missing intermediate directories recursively.
`os.listdir(path)` returns names of files/directories at the specified path; without a path it uses the current working directory.

explanation.ar: `w` truncates existing content before writing; `a` appends at the end without removing existing content.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to choose overwrite or append behavior?

options.text: os.getcwd() / os.chdir(path)
"w" vs "a"
os.mkdir() / os.makedirs()
os.listdir(path)

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. `"w" vs "a"` is the course-aligned choice for this task: choose overwrite or append behavior.

questions.question: Which mode preserves existing content and writes at the end?

options.text: w
r
a
x always

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `Write vs Append` behavior: `w` truncates existing content before writing; `a` appends at the end without removing existing content.

questions.question: A learner opens an important log in `w` mode when they intend to preserve old entries. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `os.getcwd() / os.chdir(path)` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `Write vs Append` has no rules.
Convert the task to `mkdir vs makedirs` without changing the logic.
Use append mode (`a`) when existing content must be kept.

explanation.ar: Use append mode (`a`) when existing content must be kept.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `CWD` according to the taught session?

options.text: The current working directory is where relative file operations are resolved; `os.getcwd()` reads it and `os.chdir()` changes it.
`os.mkdir()` creates one directory; `os.makedirs()` can create missing intermediate directories recursively.
`os.listdir(path)` returns names of files/directories at the specified path; without a path it uses the current working directory.
`os.remove()` deletes a file; `os.rmdir()` removes an empty directory.

explanation.ar: The current working directory is where relative file operations are resolved; `os.getcwd()` reads it and `os.chdir()` changes it.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to inspect or change the current working directory?

options.text: os.mkdir() / os.makedirs()
os.getcwd() / os.chdir(path)
os.listdir(path)
os.remove() / os.rmdir()

explanation.ar: `os.getcwd() / os.chdir(path)` is the course-aligned choice for this task: inspect or change the current working directory.

questions.question: Which function returns the current working directory?

options.text: os.listdir()
os.remove()
os.getcwd()
os.stat()

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. The trace follows the taught `CWD` behavior: The current working directory is where relative file operations are resolved; `os.getcwd()` reads it and `os.chdir()` changes it.

questions.question: A learner assumes the CWD must always equal the directory where the script file itself is stored. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `os.mkdir() / os.makedirs()` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `CWD` has no rules.
Convert the task to `listdir` without changing the logic.
Treat the CWD as the active operating directory; the source notes it is not necessarily the script-file location.

explanation.ar: Treat the CWD as the active operating directory; the source notes it is not necessarily the script-file location.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `mkdir vs makedirs` according to the taught session?

options.text: `os.mkdir()` creates one directory; `os.makedirs()` can create missing intermediate directories recursively.
`os.listdir(path)` returns names of files/directories at the specified path; without a path it uses the current working directory.
`os.remove()` deletes a file; `os.rmdir()` removes an empty directory.
The source covers permissions/metadata (`chmod`, `chown`, `stat`) plus `exists`, `getsize`, and `rename`.

explanation.ar: `os.mkdir()` creates one directory; `os.makedirs()` can create missing intermediate directories recursively.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to create a single directory or a recursive directory path?

options.text: os.listdir(path)
os.mkdir() / os.makedirs()
os.remove() / os.rmdir()
os.stat() / os.path.exists() / os.path.getsize() / os.rename()

explanation.ar: `os.mkdir() / os.makedirs()` is the course-aligned choice for this task: create a single directory or a recursive directory path.

questions.question: Which function is taught for recursively creating intermediate directories?

options.text: os.mkdir() only
os.remove()
os.makedirs()
os.getcwd()

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `mkdir vs makedirs` behavior: `os.mkdir()` creates one directory; `os.makedirs()` can create missing intermediate directories recursively.

questions.question: A learner uses `os.mkdir()` for a deep path whose intermediate directories do not exist. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `os.listdir(path)` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `mkdir vs makedirs` has no rules.
Convert the task to `remove vs rmdir` without changing the logic.
Use `os.makedirs()` when intermediate directories need to be created.

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. Use `os.makedirs()` when intermediate directories need to be created.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `listdir` according to the taught session?

options.text: `os.listdir(path)` returns names of files/directories at the specified path; without a path it uses the current working directory.
`os.remove()` deletes a file; `os.rmdir()` removes an empty directory.
The source covers permissions/metadata (`chmod`, `chown`, `stat`) plus `exists`, `getsize`, and `rename`.
`open(path, mode)` opens a file; default mode is read (`r`) if omitted.

explanation.ar: `os.listdir(path)` returns names of files/directories at the specified path; without a path it uses the current working directory.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to list files and directories?

options.text: os.remove() / os.rmdir()
os.listdir(path)
os.stat() / os.path.exists() / os.path.getsize() / os.rename()
open("file.txt", "r")

explanation.ar: `os.listdir(path)` is the course-aligned choice for this task: list files and directories.

questions.question: What does `os.listdir()` use when no directory argument is supplied?

options.text: The script source file only
The root directory always
The current working directory
A random folder

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `listdir` behavior: `os.listdir(path)` returns names of files/directories at the specified path; without a path it uses the current working directory.

questions.question: A learner expects `os.listdir()` to recursively walk every nested directory automatically. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `os.remove() / os.rmdir()` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `listdir` has no rules.
Convert the task to `File Metadata & Paths` without changing the logic.
Use it for the specified directory listing as taught; do not assume recursive traversal.

explanation.ar: Use it for the specified directory listing as taught; do not assume recursive traversal.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `remove vs rmdir` according to the taught session?

options.text: `os.remove()` deletes a file; `os.rmdir()` removes an empty directory.

`open(path, mode)` opens a file; default mode is read (`r`) if omitted.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to delete a file or an empty directory appropriately?

os.remove() / os.rmdir()

questions.question: Which function removes an empty directory?

os.getcwd()
os.rmdir()
os.stat()

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. The trace follows the taught `remove vs rmdir` behavior: `os.remove()` deletes a file; `os.rmdir()` removes an empty directory.

questions.question: A learner calls `os.remove()` on a directory path. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `os.stat() / os.path.exists() / os.path.getsize() / os.rename()` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `remove vs rmdir` has no rules.
Convert the task to `open() & Modes` without changing the logic.
Use `os.remove()` for files and `os.rmdir()` for empty directories.

questions.question: Which `os.stat()` attribute represents file size in bytes?

options.text: st_mtime
st_mode
st_size
name
